HuMCal is model-agnostic and baseline-safe on the calibration split: its optimized loss weakly dominates any fixed-weight rule over the same subgroup set, including uniform weighting, post-stratification, and the best single subgroup. We evaluate HuMCal in a revealed-preference market-structure application using U.S. bank-card transactions and in a public-opinion application using Pew survey data. Across both settings, HuMCal improves alignment on the calibration split relative to all fixed-weight baselines. Out of sample, source-learned weights outperform heuristic baselines across time, geography, industry, and topic in the large majority of evaluations, although transfer is empirical rather than guaranteed. Recalibration with newer LLM checkpoints often improves alignment further. These results suggest that HuMCal can serve as a scalable calibration tool for LLM-based measurement when collecting fresh benchmark data for each target setting is costly.

journal_feed.title: Experimental Evidence on Structural State Dependence in Demand
journal_feed.abstract: The paper provides nonparametric estimates of structural state dependence from a natural field experiment for 223 brands.

journal_feed.title: Injunctive Norms Outperform Reciprocity: Tip Request Messages Can Increase Tipping Without Reducing Demand
journal_feed.abstract: Tip request messages are marketing communications that can help digital platforms balance customer spending with worker effort and compensation. We report the first field experiments manipulating tip request message content, analyzing 435,969 transactions. We test how three appeals based on tipping motivations–injunctive norms (“It’s customary to leave a tip for the seller’s service”), personalized reciprocity and impersonal reciprocity–affect tipping and future demand in a global freelance marketplace. On the web, first exposures to the injunctive norms message increased new buyers’ tipping rate by 11.8 percentage points (p.p.), and repeat buyers’ tipping rate by 6.8 p.p. In the app, first exposures to the injunctive norms message increased tipping rate by 2.5 p.p. for new buyers and 1.4 p.p. for repeat buyers. Treatment effects on tipping increase with transaction order price. The norms and personalized reciprocity messages increased subsequent orders and spending in the web experiment, and did not significantly change repatronage in the app experiment, suggesting that effective tipping prompts need not reduce future business. Overall, tip request messages can motivate customer tipping to better incentivize and compensate gig workers, but optimization requires careful testing.

journal_feed.title: The Problem of Ignoring the Ignorability Assumption in Advertising Measurement: A Matrix Completion Solution
journal_feed.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly rely on algorithms for decision-making. A canonical success story is online advertising, where platforms use algorithmic auctions to allocate ads efficiently and maximize revenue. Another pillar of these platforms’ long-term success is accurate causal measurement of advertising effectiveness. While randomized experiments remain the gold standard, their high cost makes observational approaches appealing to both platforms and advertisers. In this paper, we show that the algorithmic nature of ad allocation fundamentally challenges causal measurement by violating the overlap assumption required for valid estimation. Even when treatment assignment is unconfounded, the deterministic structure of auctions implies that many users receive ads with near-zero or near-one probability, leading to biased estimates of ad effectiveness. We develop a novel framework that interprets this lack of overlap as a missing data problem and leverages variation across multiple advertising campaigns using matrix completion to recover causal estimates. Using both simulated and real advertising data, we demonstrate that our approach accurately recovers ad effects at aggregate and individual levels and substantially improves targeting efficiency, offering a scalable solution for causal advertising measurement in algorithmic markets. We conclude with a discussion of managerial implications and potential extensions to other algorithmic decision-making settings.

journal_feed.title: Color me aroused while keeping the cool
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Drawing on visual complexity theory and the arousal properties of color, this paper challenges the prevailing assumption that only warm (longer wavelength) or highly saturated colors can induce arousal in consumers. Instead, we propose a novel pathway: multicolor logos with cool hues can elicit arousal through triggering curiosity. Across a total of eight experiments (seven preregistered with a total of 1,724 participants recruited), of which six experiments are reported in the main text, including a behavioral lab study employing biometric measures (eye tracking, galvanic skin response, pupil dilation), and three studies utilizing real product choices, we consistently find that multicolor cool logos are more arousing than single cool color designs. This heightened, curiosity-driven arousal subsequently impacts marketing outcomes, including willingness to pay and choice. These findings offer marketers alternative strategies for inducing arousal in brand communications and provide actionable guidelines for effectively designing logos.

journal_feed.title: Spoiler alert! Watch movies before they are spoiled
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Incentive Design for Sales Managers: Impact on Resource Allocation and Performance
journal_feed.abstract: Many firms struggle to design effective incentives for sales managers . Yet despite a vast literature on salespeople’s incentives, little theoretical or empirical research has examined managers’ incentive structures. The authors address a common dilemma that firms face: Should managers’ incentives be based on achieving an aggregate target ( Aggregate Target Scheme , ATS) or instead be linked to the target achievement of each individual territory or salesperson ( Individual Target Scheme , ITS)? A quasi-experiment reveals that, despite ATS’s flexibility and apparent alignment with firm objectives, an ATS-to-ITS transition improved performance , with larger gains among lower-performing and higher-span territories. A scenario-based experiment with sales managers suggests that these effects may stem from the reallocation of resources from high to low performers but provides no evidence of an increase in managers’ overall resource investment. A survey of sales leaders indicates that a sales star bias —a managerial tendency to overallocate resources toward high performers relative to their marginal returns—likely drives suboptimal resource allocation under the flexible ATS. Finally, a supplementary field study documents that, following an ATS-to-ITS transition, managers increased joint fieldwork , especially with the lowest performers, and performance again improved. These results provide insights into managerial incentive design and offer guidance for firms.

journal_feed.title: Numerical gap effect in multigenerational brand names: The role of perceived innovation momentum
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

journal_feed.title: Sustainability in marketing: A systematic analysis and future research agenda
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

journal_feed.title: Common ownership and consumer welfare
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Rival firms with shared institutional investors (i.e., common owners) may compete less aggressively, potentially harming consumer welfare. Yet, research on common ownership has primarily focused on firm performance, often overlooking welfare outcomes or revealing contradictory results. This paper adopts a strategic network perspective to examine how common ownership affects firms’ service quality and pricing levels, which directly impact consumer welfare, and how customer and competitor factors that alter the focus of competitive strategy moderate these effects. To test the hypotheses, the authors analyze a rich, multi-market dataset of U.S. airline firms from 1995 to 2025. Findings reveal that competing firms with higher common ownership tend to have lower service quality and set higher prices. However, this effect is attenuated for firms with high customer-asset value and amplified among rivals competing across multiple markets. The findings demonstrate common ownership’s influence on firms’ marketing mix strategies and offer actionable insights for managers, policymakers, and investors.

journal_feed.title: Managing the dual nature of customer engagement in product innovation: A sensegiving and sensemaking perspective
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: The Dark Side of Competition for Market Share: Competitive Pressure May Trigger Corporate Misconduct
journal_feed.abstract: There is an ongoing debate about the role of market share and market share–based competition in shaping corporate behavior and performance. This study advances the discussion by analyzing how a firm’s specific competitive situation drives corporate misconduct and how such misconduct affects future market share. Based on a theory-in-use approach, the authors propose the Theory of Market Share–Based Competitive Pressure (TMCP) and introduce four new market share–based constructs that reflect different dimensions of competitive pressure. Using a global sample of 2,145 firms across 254 industries over 11 years, they find that firms that are closer to market leadership and more closely followed by competitors are more prone to misconduct. The results demonstrate that misconduct systematically weakens the very market positions that created the pressure in the first place, with particularly strong penalties for environmental and governance–related misconduct incidents. Importantly, organizational characteristics such as compensation design, board composition, and marketing capabilities condition the extent to which competition translates into corporate misconduct. Together, these findings demonstrate that while misconduct may appear as a shortcut to defend competitive positions, it ultimately undermines them, and there are ways to reduce incentives for misconduct in the first place.
journal_feed.subfield: Organizational Behavior and Human Resource Management

journal_feed.title: The Effects of Search Interface on Consumer Preferences: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
journal_feed.abstract: Digital platforms commonly rely on refinement tools (e.g., filters and sorters) to help users navigate large product assortments. While these tools are designed to reduce search friction, they also shape how consumers explore and what they come to value. Drawing on Information Foraging Theory, we examine how the design of search interfaces influences consumer preferences and market outcomes by altering the cost structure of information paths. In a randomized online experiment with 1,200 participants searching for headphones on a custom-built e-commerce site, we manipulated access to faceted filters to induce variation in search behavior. Results show that limiting faceted filters led consumers toward higher-priced purchases and more balanced attribute preferences, and reduced market concentration. Participants in the treated conditions, who lacked filter options, adapted their search strategies by using more sorting and browsing more; in particular, the increased exploration on product listing pages was much larger than the increased exploitation on product detail pages. Further analysis confirms that these adapted search behaviors were associated with changes in treated participants' preferences, compared to control participants with unrestricted filters. Our findings demonstrate that search interface design can construct, rather than merely reveal, consumer preferences; subtle interface changes can guide consumer behavior, encourage product exploration, and influence market outcomes.

journal_feed.title: Return on AI (RoAI): A framework for assessing AI investments in the marketing organization
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping marketing as firms increasingly delegate activities and decisions previously performed by marketers to AI systems. As AI assumes a greater role in market-facing decisions, understanding the value firms realize from these investments becomes increasingly important. Building on marketing accountability and resource-based theory, we develop a Return on AI (RoAI) framework that conceptualizes AI investment through the people, processes, and capabilities that enable its deployment and governance. RoAI evaluates incremental benefit while accounting for value retention, evidence durability, and the full costs of deployment over time. The framework identifies a distinctive consequence of delegated judgment, wherein AI can improve current performance while reducing the experiential practice through which marketers develop and maintain the judgment required to evaluate and redirect the AI solution. This mechanism helps explain heterogeneity in AI returns across firms and over time. We develop seven testable predictions and an agenda for research on creating, appropriating, and sustaining value from AI.

journal_feed.title: Identifying and managing milestones in consumers’ goal journeys
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Understanding consumers’ holistic journeys as unfolding events is paramount for managing service design and delivery. Touchpoints, “moments of truth” and critical incident research primarily focus on firm-facing events and consumers’ evaluations of firm encounters, rather than critical events in consumers’ own goal pursuit. This article introduces and uncovers the significance of milestone events in consumers’ journeys. Milestones are significant events that mark a major step or turning point in a consumer’s journey. Multi-stage, multi-context qualitative consumer journey research is used to inductively identify the key features and implications of milestones. They are distinct from other service events and consequential for consumers’ lives. This research fills a significant research gap in understanding consumer goal journeys. Identifying and understanding consumers’ milestone events enables service firms to support and improve goal progression; increase confidence in success; help consumers prepare for and interpret milestone outcomes; and manage risk by adjusting or pivoting from the goal.

journal_feed.title: Synthetic diversity: Racial depictions influence consumer responses to AI ‐generated models in advertising
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract As brands seek to increase racial representation in their advertising, many are turning to AI‐generated images of humans (i.e., synthetic models) as a scalable solution. This research demonstrates that consumer reactions to synthetic models are asymmetric, depending on the racial identity being depicted. Across five studies, we demonstrate that disclosing the AI‐generated nature of models lowers firm evaluations when the featured models are from racially underrepresented groups (e.g., Black, Hispanic, and Asian models), but not when they are White. This effect is driven by reduced perceptions of the authenticity of the firm's inclusion efforts, which in turn elevate inferences of manipulative intent. Importantly, these negative effects can be mitigated when consumers are informed that the firm is owned by members of the depicted racial community, suggesting that credible signals of authentic community ties can neutralize the evaluative penalty of AI disclosure. Our findings extend research on racialized depictions in advertising by identifying synthetic depiction as a novel threat to the evaluative benefits of minority representation, and by theorizing why this threat operates asymmetrically by race. More broadly, our results highlight that technological innovations in advertising cannot be divorced from the social and historical contexts that shape their meaning.

journal_feed.title: AI in Disguise—Quasi-Experimental Analysis of a Large-Scale Deployment of AI-Generated Ads
journal_feed.abstract: As Taboola prepared to launch its GenAI Ad Maker, a tool that lets advertisers create ad images within the platform, it faced a consequential question about whether AI-generated ad images would perform well with real consumers, and under what conditions. Working with Taboola, we construct a quasi-experimental comparison of 4,633 ‘sibling ads,’ meaning AI-generated and human-made images launched by the same advertisers, in identical campaign settings, at the same time. These ads span more than 369 million impressions and 2.5 million clicks. We do not find a detectable average click-through-rate disadvantage for AI-generated images relative to their human-made siblings. However, this average masks an important boundary condition: ads with AI-generated images outperform human-made ads when the AI images do not ‘look like AI.’ We identify key visual features influencing consumers’ perceptions of whether an ad looks AI-generated. While AI generates sharper, clearer, and less blurry images with larger faces, consumers associate these features with human-made ads. On the other hand, in line with consumers’ expectations, aesthetics, lower warmth, and intense color saturation in ads signal AI generation. These findings support Taboola’s roll-out communication, advertiser guidance, and continued refinement of the GenAI Ad Maker.

journal_feed.title: The Motivational Paradox: How Aspirational-Goal Communications Influence Sales Performance and Information Acquisition
journal_feed.abstract: This study examines how aspirational-goal communications influence sales agents’ performance and information-seeking behavior. In a field experiment across 100 stores in Sweden, agents in the treatment group received daily personalized text messages with aspirational sales goals tailored to their prior performance. Results show that these communications increase sales performance, particularly among low-performing agents, primarily through higher unit sales. At the same time, they reduce agents’ willingness to monitor within-day sales progress—reflecting the ostrich effect—which can adversely affect performance. Information acquisition, in the form of sales-progress monitoring, typically aids effort provision, but aspirational-goal communications suppress such behavior, complicating performance management. These findings highlight the dual effects of aspirational-goal communications: while they enhance motivation, they may also prompt information avoidance. The study contributes to research on goal setting and sales management by clarifying the trade-offs in designing effective motivational and communication strategies.
journal_feed.subfield: Organizational Behavior and Human Resource Management

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Expanding Markets or Capturing Share? The Competitive Effects of Subscriptions on Spending in Restaurant Delivery
journal_feed.abstract: Subscription programs are increasingly central to platform strategy, but their effects on competitors and category demand remain unclear. The authors study restaurant delivery subscriptions using individual-level transaction data on Postmates Unlimited, the first widely available U.S. subscription program in the category, and DoorDash's later DashPass program. Using a matched, staggered difference-in-differences design, they find that signing up for Postmates Unlimited is associated with a 90.4% increase in spending at the focal firm, with no significant average change in competing-firm spending and no offsetting decline in adjacent food categories, consistent with category expansion. Competitive effects depend on customers' prior platform usage. For “singlehomers” (who only used Postmates prior to subscribing), subscribing is associated with increased spending at both the focal firm and competing platforms, even after cancellation. For “multihomers” (who had also previously used competing platforms), the focal-firm effect is larger, and competing-firm spending falls while customers remain subscribed; after cancellation, the focal-firm lift persists, but the decrease in competitor spending does not. DashPass results are broadly similar, but customers with prior Postmates subscription experience show little increase in category spending. Together, these findings suggest subscriptions can both expand markets and capture share, depending on prior platform usage and subscription experience.

journal_feed.title: Pet-owner synchrony: Operationalization, application, and implications
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Despite the pet industry’s significant economic and social importance, academic attention to this sector of the economy has been limited. Rather than focusing solely on the household demographics of pet ownership or the attitudinal components of the pet-owner relationship, we explore actual purchase decisions of pet owners. In this study, we examine pet-owner synchrony, a behavioral operationalization of pet-owner relationships that is grounded in attachment theory, anthropomorphism, and the extended self. Utilizing scanner data from 875,853 market baskets including 23 million transactions collected from a regional supermarket chain, we analyze cross-category co-occurrence patterns within shopping baskets. Our analysis reveals affinities, or parallels, in pet owners’ purchases of health and wellness products and hedonic products for both themselves and their pets, which we attribute to pet-owner synchrony. We identify two moderators that influence the strength of pet-owner synchrony: pet type (cat versus dog) and the presence of young children in the household. In addition, we evaluate how basket size, holidays, and price elasticities impact pet-owner synchrony. Our findings deliver useful insights into pet-owner relationships, have direct implications for retail and manufacturing managers, and yield recommendations for public policy.

journal_feed.title: Marketing misinformation in the age of AI
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract We shine a spotlight on marketing misinformation—claims about products and brands that contradict or distort verifiable facts. Misinformation may be created unintentionally or intentionally by companies, competitors, customers, or third parties seeking to harm companies or consumers. We focus on the role of AI in creating, obfuscating, and disseminating misinformation in the form of text, audio, images, and videos generated using large language models. This type of information can pose a substantial risk for brand safety. Consumers may be aware that AI can generate misinformation but may lack the ability to guard against it. We discuss how different stakeholders in the information ecosystem can help in the prevention and correction of misinformation and propose a future research agenda in this critical and fast‐growing area.

journal_feed.title: The ripple effects of customer orientation: Personal, vicarious, and temporal pathways to frontline employee well-being
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.subfield: Organizational Behavior and Human Resource Management

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Correcting omitted-variable bias without instruments: An ICA-based alternative to Gaussian copula methods
journal_feed.abstract: This paper proposes an instrument-free correction for omitted-variable bias and overcomes a key limitation of Gaussian copula control function (GCCF) approaches. Omitted-variable bias is the most common source of endogeneity in marketing, and many articles apply GCCF to address it. Yet GCCF require a nonlinear regressor-error relation, whereas textbooks assume linear, additive relationships between regressors and omitted variables. The authors prove that GCCF is biased in classical omitted-variable settings. Extant articles that address omitted-variables with GCCF also show language cues implicitly assuming linear relationships, which invalidate the use of GCCF. The proposed endogeneity correction is tailored to this prominent case, utilizing independent component analysis (ICA). It assumes a latent normally distributed component that additively influences both the endogenous regressor and the error. This can be interpreted as the sum of omitted variables, which, according to the Central Limit Theorem, add up to a normal distribution. Through ICA, this component is identified and extracted from the endogenous regressor, rendering the regression model free of endogeneity and enabling causal inference. The paper proves that the model is point-identified despite endogeneity due to omitted variables, that the proposed estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and that Jackknife resampling yields valid standard errors.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: The Role of Digital Ad Clutter in Ad Viewership and Memory
journal_feed.abstract: Advertisers face an increasingly cluttered digital ecosystem where customer attention matters. Despite this, the extent to which digital advertising clutter influences ad viewership remains unclear. This paper presents three separate eye-tracking experiments (subjects: N = 99, N = 250, and N = 575) using over a dozen custom-built web pages to better understand how digital ad clutter affects consumers’ viewing of digital ads. Across experiments, we show that increased clutter led consumers to allocate more attention to the overall advertising space and adjust how they distribute viewership across ad positions. A complementary survey revealed that clutter also reduced ad memory and recall for individual ads. We discuss the implications for advertisers and publishers regarding ad pricing and placement in crowded digital environments.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Why are products so similar despite diverse consumer needs? The interplay between advertising and horizontal product differentiation
journal_feed.abstract: Firms are often less differentiated than standard price-competition models predict. We explain this gap by showing how firms can use informative or reminder advertising to soften competition. When firms choose locations, advertising, and prices endogenously, they may choose to soften price competition through limited advertising rather than greater product differentiation, allowing them to locate closer together while limiting price competition. This outcome of low advertising and central collocation is especially likely when advertising costs are high. We also observe that partially-differentiated equilibria, with one firm locating centrally and the other at an edge, and full differentiation, can each emerge under certain conditions. Thus, firms endogenously choose a mix of advertising and product differentiation to moderate price competition. Further, the shape of travel costs influences the equilibrium outcome. If the disutility from distance is highly convex, such as occurs when consumer preferences exhibit satisficing, central collocation becomes the unique equilibrium when more consumers are concentrated at the edge locations. However, when the disutility from distance is linear, having more customers located towards the edge locations makes collocation less likely. Overall, the interaction of advertising costs, consumer preferences, and location choices help explain why firms often forgo product differentiation.

journal_feed.title: Music Marketing with Generative AI
journal_feed.abstract: The multibillion-dollar music industry faces severe content creation bottlenecks, making multimedia marketing assets prohibitively costly for smaller artists. This practice paper introduces a Marketing Asset Generation Engine (MAGE) that can produce over 700 million video ad variations reflecting each artist’s visual identity using only a music track’s audio and album cover as inputs. Collaborating with one of the world’s largest music labels, we conduct four preregistered field studies with over 11 million impressions across 75 campaigns for 33 music tracks on TikTok and Meta to validate MAGE. First, pooled across studies, MAGE-generated ads significantly outperform human-designed ads on TikTok with on average 26% higher click-through rates and 10% higher engagement, while we do not detect statistically significant performance differences on Meta, all at 98% lower production cost. Second, neither marketing professionals nor laypeople can reliably identify winning ads such that random sampling of MAGE’s outputs performs as well as human-curated selections. In contrast, an AI-in-the-loop system trained on past performance data can predict pre-launch which MAGE-generated ads will perform best for specific audience segments. These findings demonstrate that generative AI democratizes music marketing by making effective, on-brand video ads accessible at scale.

journal_feed.title: From Data to Decisions: Marketing Analytics, Mental Performance, and Firm Growth in an Emerging Market
journal_feed.abstract: Using a field experiment with 550 Rwandan firms, we show marketing analytics causally enhances entrepreneurs’ cognition and raises firm sales and profits.

journal_feed.title: Can Facebook Ads Prevent Malaria? Two Field Experiments in India
journal_feed.abstract: Two field experiments evaluate a nationwide Facebook malaria prevention campaign in India, finding effects concentrated in urban, more advantaged populations.

journal_feed.title: Exploitation in the marketplace: A consumer behavior perspective
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract This paper examines exploitation in the marketplace from a consumer behavior perspective. We define marketplace exploitation as occurring when one party leverages structural and/or situational resource asymmetries to extract disproportionate value in ways that undermine fairness or autonomy, even when exchanges appear voluntary and mutually beneficial. We distinguish marketplace exploitation from related concepts including fairness, deception, and discrimination, arguing that it centers on the morally problematic use of contextual advantage. Adopting a dual lens, we develop conceptual frameworks for both firm‐to‐consumer exploitation (e.g., price gouging, dark patterns) and consumer‐to‐firm exploitation (e.g., free trial abuse, exploiting firm mistakes). These frameworks delineate how structural and situational asymmetries give rise to objective exploitative acts, when such acts are perceived as exploitative, and how they shape emotional, cognitive, and behavioral responses. We synthesize a research agenda and outline methodological approaches for studying the antecedents, perceptions, and consequences of exploitation. This work contributes to consumer psychology by conceptualizing marketplace exploitation as both a subjective psychological experience and a strategic marketplace behavior, with implications for theory, policy, and ethical firm practices.
journal_feed.subfield: Organizational Behavior and Human Resource Management

journal_feed.title: Can green innovations enhance competitive advantage?
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Sustainable New Product Introductions (SNPIs) enable firms to meet consumers’ increasing demand for sustainable options while addressing rising expectations for corporate environmental responsibility. This study demonstrates that SNPIs can also strengthen brands by enhancing brand equity. Drawing on signaling theory, we propose that SNPIs serve as product-based sustainability signals that enhance brand equity by generating social goodwill. A staggered event study of the initial launch of a sustainable product line by a major laundry detergent brand shows that SNPIs can increase parent-brand equity. A complementary analysis of subsequent SNPIs across 15 leading brands in 12 retail chains reveals that this effect is moderated by parent firms' ethical reputation and retail chains' sustainable assortment share. These findings advance our understanding of whether and under what conditions sustainable products serve as credible signals of environmental responsibility and enhance brand equity.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: The Collecting Mindset: Viewing Purchasing as Collecting Enhances Acquisition Experience and Product Desirability
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Managers often struggle to make acquisition processes engaging. While the dominant approach to reducing search costs has been to streamline the acquisition process, seven preregistered studies plus one supplemental study (N = 3,306) reveal an alternative pathway: Prompting consumers to view purchasing as “collecting” by positioning products as additions to their own collections, rather than as ad hoc purchases, improves consumers’ acquisition experience and increases product desirability. The authors demonstrate that activating such a collecting mindset shifts consumers’ psychological focus of the shopping process from securing a standalone product to instead investing in advancing their collection, thereby making them derive positive experience utility from the process, and in turn, elevating the desirability of the sought products. This research also offers practical guidance on how marketers can maximize the effectiveness of activating a collecting mindset: (i) encouraging active engagement in search, (ii) ensuring that search yields products that meaningfully advance the collection, and (iii) aligning the collection with an identity consumers value, as the effect may otherwise attenuate or reverse. These findings advance theory on everyday collecting and consumer search, and show how retailers and brands can strategically turn purchasing into a more positive acquisition experience that enhances product desirability.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Lifestage Bias: How the Visual Representation of Product Lifespan Shapes Replacement Timing
journal_feed.abstract: To guide consumers’ decisions regarding when to replace products such as water filters, printer ink cartridges, and engine oil, companies often provide visualizations of the product’s lifespan. We document a lifestage bias in which representing a product’s lifespan with more (vs. fewer) visually distinct stages increases replacement intentions even when the product’s actual usage is the same. The effect emerges because a greater number of visually distinct stages leads consumers to mentally simulate previous use, thus enhancing the perception that a product has progressed through its lifespan and encouraging product replacement. Ten studies document lifestage bias and provide support (via mediation and moderation) for the underlying usage simulation mechanism. Notably, lifestage bias is eliminated when stages are represented non-visually or when stages are not visually distinct. Furthermore, lifestage bias is attenuated when product deterioration can be observed directly. These findings provide important insights into how consumers make product replacement timing decisions. Adjusting the number of distinct stages in product replacement guides offers firms and policymakers a practical tool to influence replacement timing—accelerating it when timely replacement is necessary for health, safety, or regulatory reasons (thus improving consumer welfare), or delaying it when items can be safely used for longer (thus reducing waste).

journal_feed.title: Populism and sustainable marketing practices: Insights from consumer-packaged goods manufacturers’ new product launches
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract While sustainable marketing practices have traditionally been grounded in stakeholder capitalism, the rise of anti-climate-action populism presents new challenges to firms’ sustainable strategies. Drawing on resource dependence theory, this study argues that anti-climate-action populism prompts firms to reduce sustainable marketing practices, specifically the use of environmentally friendly packaging in new product launches. However, we propose that subnational formal and informal institutions, such as economic freedom and cultural tightness, attenuate this effect. To test these hypotheses, we employ a quasi-natural experimental design, using the announcement of the United States’ exit from the Paris Agreement to analyze its impact on sustainable marketing practices, based on a global sample of product launches by consumer-packaged goods manufacturers. Our difference-in-differences analysis supports these hypotheses. This study advances the understanding of the dynamic relationship between populism and subnational institutions, highlighting how different institutional pillars shape firms’ sustainable marketing strategies.

journal_feed.title: The Identification of the Dynamic Discrete-Choice Model with Stockpiling
journal_feed.abstract: We study the identification of the discount factor for dynamic discrete-choice (DDC) models of demand with stockpiling of a storable good. We show that the DDC has built-in exclusion restrictions that set-identify the discount factor without requiring any auxiliary assumptions. We compare this approach to previous work that assumes auxiliary structure on the storage cost function, clarifying how such structure generates exclusion restrictions and the corresponding data moments used for identification. Our key results show that these auxiliary restrictions are not necessary for identification; but that they are testable and can be included to achieve point identification and improve statistical efficiency. Using a case study of laundry detergent from earlier published work, we find a mean discount factor estimate of $0.957$, rejecting myopic models of choice in favor of the dynamic model. In counterfactual simulations, we show that some of the promotional lift during a discount period is indeed due to forward-buying. However, we predict considerably higher incremental sales compared to a standard discrete-choice model, which predicts that promotional discounts mainly cause substitution between brands. These results contribute to the long-standing discussion about the effectiveness of price promotions.

journal_feed.title: From Live to Recording: Consumer Demand and Response to Price Across the Livestreaming Lifecycle
journal_feed.abstract: Using data from a knowledge-sharing platform that sells recorded versions of paid livestreams, this paper finds that demand is surprisingly more price sensitive before the event than after, which is explained partly by consumer self-selection and the lower quality uncertainty once the livestream ends.

journal_feed.title: Visual Plant Imagery and Property Valuation: A Descriptive Analysis
journal_feed.abstract: Online home profiles with more plant imagery are associated with higher property valuations, even after accounting for extensive property, neighborhood, listing, and market factors.

journal_feed.title: Signaling uniqueness: The psycholinguistic effect of language precision on product perceptions
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract This research reveals a psycholinguistic effect whereby more precise words in product communications increase consumer perceptions of product uniqueness. Drawing on Categorization Theory, the authors propose that more precise words in product descriptions are situated deeper within their semantic categories and denote narrower subsets of referents, thereby eliciting perceptions of product uniqueness. [Correction added on 15 October 2026, after first online publication: The reference in the preceding sentence has been removed.] Four experiments provide robust evidence supporting the “precise‐unique effect” and its underlying psycholinguistic mechanism driven by categorical depth. The findings further suggest that consumers' need for product uniqueness moderates the downstream effects of language precision on perceived attractiveness and behavioral intention via perceived uniqueness. This research contributes to the growing literature on language effects in consumer psychology and provides practical implications for making strategic lexical choices that enhance product positioning and differentiation.

journal_feed.title: Symbolic promotions: Conceptualization and empirical investigation
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Symbolic promotions are an increasingly prevalent marketing practice globally, yet little is known about how or when they influence consumer behavior. We conceptualize symbolic promotions as a distinct type of sales promotion that creates value by reinforcing consumers' social identity through shared group membership rather than by providing economic incentives, such as reward-based promotions, or supporting distant others, such as cause-related marketing promotions (CMPs). We investigate the effectiveness of symbolic promotions and their underlying mechanisms using a multimethod approach. A nine-year longitudinal field study of daily sales for 22,084 books demonstrates that an existing symbolic promotion ("On August 12, I buy a Quebec book!") generates a substantial increase in sales, with stronger effects for lesser-known brands than for well-known brands. A follow-up experiment uncovers the unique mechanisms underlying these effects, showing that symbolic promotions stimulate curiosity and community rootedness, which in turn enhance multiple types of behavioral intentions, i.e., the likelihood of participating in the promotion, sharing it on social media, and future brand consideration. Together, these findings position symbolic promotions as a distinct, complementary addition to firms’ promotional portfolios, and demonstrate how firms can leverage shared identities to create value beyond traditional monetary incentives, with implications for various stakeholders.

journal_feed.title: Diagnosing image-ad success: An interpretable and scalable framework for liking, sharing, and memorability
journal_feed.venue: International Journal of Research in Marketing

journal_feed.title: How should companies use empathetic robots to drive consumer engagement, and under what conditions?
journal_feed.venue: International Journal of Research in Marketing
journal_feed.abstract: How does consumers' perception of robot empathy facilitate their engagement with robotic services? To address this question, we investigate the experiences of actual robot users across various service settings. Drawing on insights from exploratory interviews, a field survey, and a series of field and lab experiments with both Japanese robot users and international consumers, our research highlights how robot empathy can enhance consumer escapism and future usage across hedonic and utilitarian settings. Our findings further show that robot empathy facilitates consumer escapism and engagement in service environments characterized by low privacy sensitivity but may hinder these outcomes when privacy concerns are high. Managers should therefore implement emotionally resonant and imagination-triggering empathetic behaviors when privacy sensitivity is low, but dial down emotional expressiveness and instead focus on neutral support and professionalism when privacy sensitivity is high. This research contributes to the growing literature on human-robot service interactions by offering actionable guidelines for designing empathetic robots.

journal_feed.title: Do relationship disruptions increase spending on product categories high in eudaimonic value?
journal_feed.abstract: Relationship disruptions such as death of a spouse and divorce are among the most impactful events in someone’s life, yet current retailing literature does not document their influence on shopping behavior. In this research, we study the effect of relational disruptions on the shift in shopping basket composition towards specific value orientations (utilitarian vs. hedonic vs. eudaimonic). Since people derive meaning from their social connections, we expect relational disruptions to shift basket-level purchases toward product categories that offer higher eudaimonic value, reflecting a search for deeper meaning. We apply difference-in-difference models combined with propensity score matching to a longitudinal dataset of U.S. households’ purchases across 998 product sub-categories and find that households experiencing such negative life events shift their purchases towards products higher in eudaimonic value—a finding we term the broken home effect. Supporting a meaning-based account, the effect attenuates when other family members are present in the household. These findings contribute to the literature on life events and retailing, and offer key managerial implications for strategic category management by showing how basket composition may reveal consumers’ eudaimonic needs.

journal_feed.title: Customer Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence (CAAI): Applications, Scale Development, and Testing
journal_feed.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming retailing, yet existing research on the extent to which individuals accept customer-facing AI-enabled retailing applications has largely relied on general technology acceptance frameworks and lacks a multidimensional, customer-centric measure tailored to retail AI contexts. Addressing this gap, the current research develops and validates a Customer Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence (CAAI) scale through a multi-study, multi-method program. The formative CAAI construct comprises eight first-order reflective dimensions: personalization, accuracy, safety, speed, convenience, humanization, friendliness, and emotionality. The 32-item full-scale and an 8-item condensed version are tested across diverse settings, demonstrating strong reliability, validity, generalizability, and predictive power. Moreover, the CAAI scale outperforms previously established measures relating to technology acceptance and artificial intelligence, providing a more precise and contextually relevant assessment of customer evaluations in retail settings. Results indicate that higher CAAI scores are associated with higher levels of word of mouth, share of usage, willingness to pay, and likelihood of adopting AI-enabled retailing applications. Thus, this paper provides a robust scale for assessing customer acceptance of AI and offers actionable guidance for both retailers and researchers.

journal_feed.title: What if you dislike the brand you promote? How creatives' brand attitudes affect promotional content
journal_feed.venue: International Journal of Research in Marketing
journal_feed.abstract: This research investigates how creators' brand attitudes influence the promotional content they create for brands. It finds that professional creatives and other promotional content creators are more likely to use functional elements and less likely to include emotional elements when they have negative (vs. positive) brand attitudes. Importantly, the effect is driven by creators with negative brand attitudes: creators who dislike a brand seek to stay rational and suppress their emotions to reduce the perceived unwanted influence of their brand attitudes. Specifically, creators hold a lay belief that their negative attitudes might be detrimental to their work and that remaining rational and suppressing emotions are appropriate strategies to mitigate this concern. This, in turn, influences the functional and emotional elements included in promotional content. The effect cannot be explained by brand characteristics, specific grounds underlying creators' brand attitudes, or task difficulty.

journal_feed.title: Consumer scheduling of experiential activities in shopping centers
journal_feed.abstract: Consumers increasingly visit shopping centers, including shopping malls and city centers, to engage in experiential activities. Consequently, retailers and shopping center managers need to understand consumer visitation preferences for these activities and how they affect consumer store visits within a center. Existing consumer store location choice theory does not account for the experiential nature of shopping and ignores the role of experiential non-shopping activities in determining consumer store choices. To amend for this, the authors propose three ways in which consumer experiential activity choices differ from store choices as traditionally conceived. First, experiential activities tend to be discretionary, which means that consumers can choose to add more activities or end their visit at any time. Second, spending time on an experiential activity may represent a benefit instead of only a cost. Third, consumers may prefer to undertake experiential activities in particular, asymmetric orders. After outlining their theory, they present a formal approach to assessing the role of experiential characteristics of activities when consumers determine which stores and other activities in a shopping center to visit. An experiment in which participants schedule a visit to their city center illustrates and supports the role of experiential activities in determining consumers’ store choices. Follow up simulations explore how store choices would change when specific shopping or entertainment activities are added to the study area.

journal_feed.title: When format boundaries collapse: Price reactions of conventional retailers to national-brand listings at hard discounters
journal_feed.abstract: Hard discounters (HDs) have become a dominant force in grocery retailing, placing increasing competitive pressure on conventional retailers (CRs). As HDs expand their assortments to include more national brands (NBs), consumers can increasingly compare branded products across retail formats, weakening one of CRs’ traditional sources of differentiation. Yet little is known about how CRs adjust their NB prices in response to HDs’ NB listings, how these responses vary across brands and product categories, and how such price adjustments affect CRs’ sales. Drawing on data from over 300 NB listings by HDs across multiple product categories and three European grocery markets, we analyze pricing responses by leading HiLo retailers and the associated sales effects. We find that, on average, CRs lower NB prices after HDs list these brands. HD listings increase CRs’ NB sales on average, with price reductions further improving these sales outcomes. Although price reductions are larger for follower brands and lower-purchase-frequency categories, they generate stronger sales responses for market-leading brands and in more frequently purchased categories. Finally, among the observed price reductions, most do not improve short-run brand sales, whereas unchanged prices are rarely associated with declining sales that could have been mitigated through lower prices.

journal_feed.title: Customer air quality perceptions: conceptualization, scale development, and validation
journal_feed.abstract: Air quality affects how consumers experience retail environments. In their efforts to monitor and manage air quality, retailers often rely on objective measures. However, those measures do not capture consumer perceptions about their nuanced, lived experiences with the air. By developing a customer-perceived air quality measure for use in retail stores, the current research aims to help retailers understand and leverage these influential perceptions. Building on retail atmospherics and air quality research, as well as established scale development procedures, the authors develop and validate a scale with items pertaining to air breathability, circulation, freshness, humidity, scent, and temperature in Studies 1a–1e. Through content validity assessments, readability tests, and item judging, they establish a reduced item pool. Study 2 refines the scale to 26 items and provides initial validation with café customers; it shows that perceived air quality predicts dwell time, which predicts spending, whereas an objective air quality indicator predicts neither. Study 3 offers further validation among supermarket customers and supports customer-perceived air quality as a distinct perceptual layer of the retail atmosphere. Study 4 provides experimental validation. The resulting AirQual scale offers highly relevant implications for both theory and managerial practice.

journal_feed.title: Planning better over buying cheaper: How households adjust grocery shopping to inflation across income groups
From recommendation to revenue: Store-level evidence on the dynamic and spatial effects of the Net Promoter Score (NPS)
journal_feed.abstract: We investigate the effects of customers’ propensity to recommend a brand measured by the Net Promoter Score (NPS) on the sales of a publicly listed UK retail firm, which is dominant in the upholstered furniture market in which relatively expensive durable products have a long replacement cycle. From reasoning about word-of-mouth transmission, we theorize that store-level NPS effects are likely to (i) be nonlinear over time and (ii) depend not only on store’s own NPS but also on the firm’s neighboring stores’ NPS. We investigate the relationship between the NPS and sales over a 48-month period, matching every UK store’s monthly sales with its monthly NPS. We advance an econometric approach to allow for the identification of a non-linear time path. We find that the NPS, operationalized by surveying established customers six months after purchase, predicts future sales. Moreover, NPS sales effects unfold over many months along an “inverted U” time path: for own-store effects, from eight months after purchase, peaking at 10 months; and for neighboring-store effects, from six months after purchase, peaking at 11 months. Quantitatively, a sustained increase in the NPS across the company gives rise to substantial financial returns.

journal_feed.title: Rating an Experience Makes People Notice How It Is Changing: Consequences for Hedonic Adaptation and Consumer Enjoyment
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Repeated measurement is common in both marketing research and practice. For example, experimenters often ask participants to evaluate multiple similar products, and service providers regularly check in to see how customers are doing. Such practices rest on the assumption that collecting more data simply reveals consumers’ experiences and preferences as they evolve over time. The present research finds that repeated measurement also shapes them. Specifically, repeatedly probing consumers about an experience draws attention to how it is changing, prompting consumers to notice incremental differences more than if they were probed less or simply left alone. This process has important consequences for hedonic adaptation and enjoyment. In contexts of negative change, repeated ratings exacerbate adaptation by making incremental declines more salient, accelerating boredom and disengagement. In contexts of positive change, repeated ratings enhance experiences by making incremental improvements more salient. Eight studies (plus eight supplemental replications; total N = 16,311), spanning diverse hedonic stimuli (including games, foods, songs, videos, and artwork) and methodological approaches (including mediation and moderation), highlight this core idea that change is amplified when ratings draw attention to it. The research discusses how repeated measurement may thereby distort understandings of hedonic decline and consumer preferences, and how to harness these insights to promote longer-lasting consumer enjoyment.

journal_feed.title: Brand-Neutral Content Marketing and Endogenous Search Prominence
journal_feed.abstract: Brand-neutral content marketing attracts consumers by addressing category-level needs without directly promoting the brand. Although this may position a firm as consumers’ first point of inquiry, it leaves consumers only partially informed about brand fit. Rivals can exploit this gap by providing brand-specific information. Using a game-theoretic framework, we examine when content marketing generates endogenous search prominence and how the resulting search dynamics shape competitive communication strategies. We show that content marketing can provide a counterintuitive competitive edge: by shaping the information structure of consumer search, it influences rival pricing incentives, giving rise to asymmetric communication equilibria sustained by an information–exploitation tradeoff that governs profit allocation between the prominent gatekeeper and the non-prominent follower. When prices cannot be credibly committed, exploitation permanently dominates and content marketing becomes the unique equilibrium strategy. Brand strength and appeal breadth further determine which firm adopts content marketing.

journal_feed.title: Growing sentimental value through object usage
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Consumers often protect their sentimentally valuable possessions by storing them away, which precludes them from being used. Across five studies, we show that usage of sentimentally valuable objects increases their sentimental value. Process evidence suggests one reason this happens: Repeatedly using a sentimentally valuable object makes the association held by the object (i.e., the source of its sentimental value) salient more frequently. This leads one to believe that such an association is more closely integrated into their self‐concept, which cyclically enhances the sentimental value of the object. We conclude by discussing the contribution of these findings to the literature, providing recommendations to marketers and consumers, and elaborating on directions for future research.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: The Double-Edged Offline Touchpoint: How Self-Pickup Stations Reshape Pure-Play E-Commerce Transactions
journal_feed.abstract: Click-and-collect services through self-pickup stations have gained popularity as an alternative to traditional home delivery in e-commerce. This fulfillment option can increase customer purchases by enhancing post-purchase convenience and reducing transaction costs. However, increased hassle costs for customers and exposure to offline competition make the net impact uncertain. This study utilizes a Synthetic Difference-in-Differences (SDID) approach to analyze individual-level transaction data from an online shopping platform in Asia. Self-pickup station openings are found to have a positive net effect on customer spending and shopping frequency on the platform, without cannibalizing home delivery. A closer examination of customer dynamics reveals that station openings stabilize the platform’s user base by reducing customer churn and deepening engagement among existing shoppers, rather than driving new user acquisition. Furthermore, these positive effects are moderated by: station accessibility, level of nearby offline competition, and product attributes. Specifically, this paper provides the first empirical evidence that the positive effect of pickup stations can be reduced, if platforms locate them close to major offline retail alternatives. These findings provide important implications for e-commerce platforms regarding self-pickup station benefits, product suitability, and location strategy to reduce the risk of customer loss to offline retailers.

journal_feed.title: Multi-stakeholder market shaping for sustainability: effort types and enactment pathways in B2B markets
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Marketing scholarship has primarily focused on influencing consumer behavior towards sustainability, yet many sustainability challenges require market-level changes across multiple stakeholders. Addressing this gap, we examine how heterogeneous stakeholders collectively shape markets for sustainability. We conduct a multi-case study of B2B markets whose impact on climate change and biodiversity is actively contested. Drawing on institutional field theory, we conceptualize market shaping for sustainability as linked to issue fields where diverse stakeholders engage to influence market trajectories. Our abductive analysis identifies four types of multi-stakeholder market-shaping efforts pursuing markedly different—at times opposing—market-level outcomes: status quo maintenance, targeted reform, infrastructure reform, and market contraction. To explain this variation, we delineate four pathways through which stakeholders enact sustainability-related issues—two for challengers and two for incumbents. By linking these pathways to intended market-level outcomes, we advance theory on market-based sustainability interventions and offer actionable insights for navigating multi-stakeholder market-shaping processes.

journal_feed.title: Thank You, Now What? How Donors Respond to Calls to Action
journal_feed.abstract: We study whether thank-you communications that charities send to past donors should include a call to action and show that the answer depends on whether the donor has already given in the current giving cycle.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: The Humanizing Power of Accents in Voicebots: When Accent-Based Humanization Increases User Engagement
journal_feed.abstract: Given that consumers often exhibit resistance toward algorithmic systems, firms face challenges in encouraging engagement with voicebots. In this paper, we find that users’ engagement with voicebots may be enhanced by endowing these tools with non-standard accents that deviate from “standard” pronunciation. Across a range of accents, languages, genders, and contexts, our data suggest that voicebots communicating with non-standard accents make the concept of human diversity salient in the users’ minds. As a result, voicebots communicating with non-standard accents are more readily anthropomorphized. This effect translates into greater preference for the non-standard accented voicebot in customer service settings, stronger support for startups leveraging accented vs. unaccented voicebots, higher willingness to pay for monthly subscriptions, and a greater likelihood of opting in to receive future updates and communications. Consistent with our theory, however, these effects do not hold when the anthropomorphism effect is either overridden by other cues or is undesirable for the consumer. Together, this work highlights the benefits of accented speech in improving human-AI interactions. We also hope that it sparks further investigation into factors that make technology more readily accepted by consumers.

journal_feed.title: Through thick and thin? When sustainable packaging design increases consumer waste generation
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Packaging decisions involve a complex balance of cost, functionality, efficiency, branding, and sustainability initiatives. One promising sustainability strategy that also reduces costs is lightweighting, a manufacturing practice aimed at reducing raw material usage. In reducing raw material use, lightweighting results in structural changes to the packaging, specifically a reduction in packaging density, which has downstream consequences on consumer disposal. When assessing packaging for disposability cues, we show packaging density drives perceptions of its quality, value, and associated feelings of waste aversion. While lightweighting reduces firms’ waste, this work finds that once low-density packaging gets into consumers’ hands, it produces more waste, as consumers are more likely to improperly trash low-density versus high-density recyclable packaging. However, prompting consumers to reconsider the value of low-density packaging can curtail this unintended wastefulness. This work highlights that even sustainable firm practices can result in unintended and unsustainable consequences.

journal_feed.title: Returnless Partial Refunds: A Large-Scale Field Experiment in E-Commerce
journal_feed.abstract: A large-scale field experiment shows AI-enabled returnless partial refunds increase customer value and reduce operating costs while raising strategic-behavior risks.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Infinite-Scrolling vs. Pagination: The Impact of Interface Layouts on Product Returns
journal_feed.abstract: Interface layout, although a fundamental and prominent aspect inherent to online interfaces, has received limited attention in consumer research. This paper explores how the two major types of interface layout (infinite scrolling and pagination) influence consumers’ product return behavior in the context of free returns, a standard policy on e-commerce sites. Across five studies featuring real websites, we show that an infinite-scrolling (versus paginated) layout increases consumers’ tendency to return purchased products. This effect occurs because infinite scrolling dampens consumers’ perceived navigational control over the website, which impairs their choice closure after making decisions, thereby increasing product return intentions. We also identify both theoretically relevant and managerially important moderators and interventions to mitigate this adverse effect of infinite scrolling, such as incorporating navigational aids (e.g., displaying sequence numbers alongside), providing affirmative feedback, and accounting for the cost of product returns. This research not only contributes to the literature on interface effects, website navigation, and product returns but also provides applied insights for marketing practitioners.

journal_feed.title: Pathways to premium: How habits and benefits shape conversion and retention in freemium subscription models
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Numerous digital services rely on freemium models, yet the mechanisms that move users from free usage to premium subscriptions remain poorly understood. This research examines how expected benefits of premium access, experienced benefits during trials, and habit development in free and premium contexts jointly shape conversion and retention. Across four empirical field studies in a freemium subscription setting, we show that habits in the free version are double‑edged: they can increase conversion by reinforcing expected benefits of the premium version, yet also anchor users in continued free usage through inertia. Habits formed while using the premium version, together with experienced premium benefits, generally support paid conversion and long‑term retention. In discounted trial settings, we further identify an inverse‑U‑shaped relationship between premium‑side habits and retention, with very strong habits associated with lower retention than moderate levels. These insights inform the design of effective freemium and trial strategies.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Political Extremism and Post-Purchase Customer–Brand Relationships
journal_feed.abstract: Political polarization continues to intensify and has inspired substantial research on how individuals’ political identities shape their behaviors as consumers. This stream of research has focused primarily on differences between those on the “left” and the “right” of the political spectrum, offering valuable insights but addressing only one dimension of polarization. The current research introduces the other, currently overlooked dimension, political extremism, and examines how individuals closer to each end of the ideological spectrum differ in post-purchase decision-making from those with weaker or moderate identities. It shows that politically extreme consumers exhibit stronger repurchase likelihood, potentially deriving benefits associated with committing to brands. However, they are also less sensitive to price increases by their chosen brands, even when viable alternatives exist, increasing the risk of overpaying and undermining their financial well-being. These effects are driven by politically extreme consumers’ beliefs in the superiority of their consumption choices and are more pronounced in the presence of threats that originate from the consumption domain (e.g., focal brand product/service failures, competitor new product launches), whereas they diminish in the presence of threats originating from the political domain (e.g., customer–focal brand political misalignment, customer–competitor political alignment).

journal_feed.title: Global Product Strategies and Cultural Promotion in the Context of Culture-Commerce Interactions
journal_feed.abstract: A global firm can strategically maintain or even leverage cultural distance despite it being costless to reduce because such distance fosters consumer cultural adaptation that boosts long-term profits, whereas cultural promotion, though not directly increasing willingness to pay, indirectly enhances profitability by deepening cultural appreciation, ultimately benefiting both the firm and consumers and suggesting that nonprofit cultural initiatives can align with profit-driven goals in global consumerism.

journal_feed.title: The Challenges of Deploying an Algorithmic Pricing Tool: Evidence from Airbnb
journal_feed.abstract: This paper examines the challenges of deploying an AI pricing tool developed by Airbnb and explores possible solutions.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Clarifying Individual Contributions: The Divisibility-Appeal Effect in Fundraising
journal_feed.abstract: Organizers often strategically design numerical information in fundraising campaigns to appeal to contributors with divergent preferences. The current research highlights the importance of jointly considering the goal amount and the requested amount in campaign design, and uncovers a “divisibility-appeal effect,” whereby consumers are more likely to contribute when the campaign’s goal amount is perceived as easily divisible by the requested amount. Seven studies, including ﬁeld, secondary data, and lab experiments, provide convergent evidence for this effect and clarify its underlying mechanism: Fundraising appeals with high (vs. low) divisibility between the goal and requested amount lead to greater perceived clarity of individual contribution toward the fundraising goal, which in turn fosters consumers’ motivation to pursue the collective goal. These findings demonstrate the influence of nuanced numerical signals in collective action contexts and highlight how consumers’ numerical cognition can be effectively utilized in real-world applications to promote the provision of public goods.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: EV Charging Availability and Grocery Store Performance
journal_feed.abstract: Grocery retailers are well-positioned to help address the shortage of EV charging infrastructure but seek insight on the implications for store performance. They lack clarity on the revenue impact of EV charging availability on their parking lots, the underlying mechanisms, and the conditions under which the effect is more pronounced. Drawing on a dataset of over 300 stores of a leading German grocery chain and utilizing a staggered Difference-in-Differences quasi-experimental design, the authors show that EV charging availability increases revenues by 3.4%. Market expansion alone cannot fully explain the effect as the authors find significant evidence for market stealing. They further find that the increase is due to more transactions, not to changes in basket size. The largest increase materializes during off-peak weekend hours. They identify several attitudinal (perceived impulsiveness, storability) and behavioral (penetration, purchase frequency) category characteristics that explain where the revenue increase comes from and provide insights into the role of various store (surface-to-parking ratio, management type) and market (e.g., local competition, apartment-to-house ratio, neighborhood wealth) characteristics. Guidance for store managers interested in increasing the benefits of having EV charging on their premises and chain managers supervising the roll-out throughout their store network is provided.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: When Consumers Prefer Point Versus Range Estimates of Product Performance
journal_feed.abstract: Product performance claims play an important role in shaping consumers’ purchase decisions. Through six preregistered studies, including one field study, the authors demonstrate that consumers’ preferences for point versus range performance estimates in common comparative purchase settings depend on whether their attention is directed toward the content of the claim or the manner of its presentation. At baseline, consumers focus on what information is communicated and prefer point over range estimates because point estimates convey greater certainty about the expected performance outcome. When consumers’ persuasion knowledge is activated, however, their attention shifts toward how information is communicated. In this mode, the format of the claim, rather than the stated performance figures, becomes relatively more informative: range estimates signal brand transparency by acknowledging the natural variability of real-world performance, enhancing perceived trustworthiness and reversing consumer preference. These effects are attenuated when products are evaluated in isolation rather than compared side by side. Collectively, these findings inform both theory and practice by revealing when and why consumers prefer point versus range estimates of product performance.

journal_feed.title: Time-Duration Asymmetries in Consumer Decision-Making
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Consumers routinely make decisions about short time periods, such as waiting for a table or deciding whether to pay for faster delivery. Such periods are often expressed by either a duration or a clock time (e.g., if it is 6:00 PM now, “Your table will be ready in 30 minutes” vs. “Your table will be ready at 6:30 PM”). Eight experiments (N = 16,604) show that these logically equivalent frames change how long a period feels, with downstream consequences for consumer decisions. Relatively short time periods feel longer when framed by duration rather than by start and end time (i.e., clock times or calendar dates), but this pattern reverses as periods get longer. This research refers to this phenomenon as time-duration asymmetry: framing an interval by its start and end time versus its duration changes how long it feels, with the direction of the effect depending on the interval’s length. This research proposes that this occurs because duration frames evoke compressive scalar representations shaped by diminishing sensitivity, whereas start–end frames situate time within structured categorical systems that attenuate compression. This research offers a unified framework for understanding how subtle differences in temporal framing shape perceptions of time and subsequent decisions.

journal_feed.title: Turning Uncertainty into Opportunity: Preference Uncertainty Can Be Beneficial When Consumers Face Outcome Uncertainty
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Consumers can experience two types of uncertainty when purchasing a product. Preference uncertainty (PU) refers to the uncertainty associated with the horizontal product benefits one desires (e.g., “How strong do I want my coffee to be?”). Outcome uncertainty (OU) refers to the uncertainty associated with the actual benefits the product will deliver (e.g., “How strong will the coffee be?”). Ideally, retailers should strive for outcome certainty (i.e., standardize the strength profile of their coffee [coffees in their line]), and help consumers achieve preference certainty (i.e., help consumers learn their ideal coffee strength), so that consumers can purchase the appropriate product with confidence (i.e., achieve a preference-outcome match). Yet there are situations where high OU is a characteristic of the product class, after controlling for quality (e.g., flavor profile of wine). When OU is high, the present research paradoxically finds that high PU leads to more purchase intent than low PU. This effect occurs because people are more optimistic that they will maximize their utility when PU is high (i.e., multiple outcomes could potentially be the best match for their preference) than low (i.e., only one outcome could be the best match for their preference).
